query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor addition of aluminum to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr improves its oxygen resistance by enabling the formation of a continuous, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale without degrading its mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr that exhibits acceptable room-temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C) but suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a small amount (e.g., around 5 atomic %) of aluminum during alloy melting to partially substitute one or more of the original refractory components.
generation.conditions: Heat treatment and oxidation testing in air at approximately 800 °C for 5 hours; mechanical evaluations performed at room temperature for ductility and at elevated temperatures (e.g., 1000 °C, under strain rates of 10^–4–10^–2 s^–1) for yield strength.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formation of a protective, slow-growing alumina (Al2O3) scale on the surface of the alloy during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum atoms preferentially oxidize at high temperatures to form a dense, adherent alumina layer that impedes further oxygen ingress. This protective layer minimizes oxidation damage without significantly altering the alloy’s bulk microstructure and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the Al-modified alloy will show lower oxidation mass gain and reduced scale spallation after a 5-hour exposure at 800 °C, while retaining comparable room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exposed under identical conditions, which exhibits rapid oxidation and scale detachment (pesting).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under oxidation conditions in air at around 800 °C for up to 5 hours, with mechanical performance evaluated at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (e.g., 1000 °C) using strain rates between 10^–4 and 10^–2 s^–1.
generation.uncertainty: The precise aluminum level to maximize oxidation resistance while maintaining phase stability and mechanical properties is not fully established and requires further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy variants: the baseline equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and an Al-modified alloy with approximately 5 at.% Al added. Subject both alloys to oxidation in air at 800 °C for 5 hours. Perform surface analyses (e.g., SEM/EDS) to characterize oxide scale formation and determine oxidation mass gain. Conduct tensile tests at room temperature and high-temperature yield strength tests at 1000 °C.
measurements: Oxidation mass gain and scale morphology (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (i.e., similar oxidation mass gain and scale spallation as the untreated alloy) or if its mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) are compromised relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

In the last few decades, the development of nickel-based superalloys has allowed a steady increase in operating temperatures of jet turbine engines, which leads to enhanced engine performance and efficiency. However, nowadays the engine operating temperatures have reached around 80% of the melting points of the materials, [1] i.e. , almost reaching the upper limit of usability, making it impossible to further increase the operating temperature. Thus, it is urgently needed to develop new materials that can withstand higher operating temperatures to achieve better performance, higher engine efficiency, and lower greenhouse gas emissions.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ].
